title: What do illustrators charge and how to build a sustainable pricing strategy on Mac
metaTitle: What do illustrators charge? A guide to pricing strategy for Mac users
description: Learn what do illustrators charge and how to develop a professional pricing strategy on your Mac to avoid burnout and underpricing.
intro: Many illustrators struggle to answer what do illustrators charge because they confuse their hourly effort with the commercial value of their work. This uncertainty is a major source of financial stress, as only 20% of illustrators report feeling fairly paid for their projects. You can fix this by shifting your focus from time-based billing to value-based licensing.
tldr: Most illustrators underprice because they focus on hours worked rather than usage rights.
Only 20% of illustrators feel fairly paid, often due to inconsistent pricing models.
Stop pricing based on survival and start using tiered licensing structures.
Audit your past projects to see which clients actually provide a sustainable income.
Use tools like Notion or Wave on your Mac to track your actual business costs.

stats.label: illustrators who have never raised their rates

blocks.text: The biggest mistake you can make is charging by the hour. When you charge by the hour, you punish yourself for becoming faster and more efficient. If you spend ten hours on a project at the start of your career, and two hours on the same project three years later, you lose money if your rate remains the same. Clients do not pay for your time. They pay for the right to use your art to make money themselves.

Psychological bias is a common cause for underpricing. Many illustrators feel that if they charge a fair market rate, they will lose the client. This fear leads to defensive pricing. You offer a discount to secure the work, but that discount signals to the buyer that your work is a commodity rather than a specialized asset. This cycle is hard to break once you establish a reputation for being the cheap option.
Simple steps to fix your pricing

items: Create a standard rate card that includes usage rights for different media.
Stop giving quotes on the phone. Send a structured proposal instead.
Review your income and expenses in Wave every month to see your real margins.
Increase your rates for new clients every six months until you find your market ceiling.
Charge a kill fee for projects that are cancelled after you start work.

blocks.text: Using your Mac to manage your business

Your Mac is more than a canvas for Photoshop. It is the hub of your business. Use Notion to build a CRM that tracks every inquiry you receive. When you get an email, use ⌘ ⌥ ⌃ ⇧ to trigger a workflow that saves the client details into your database. Keep your invoice templates in a dedicated folder in Finder, sorted by year and client name.

If you are unsure how to calculate your overhead, use a spreadsheet. Open Numbers and list every subscription, software license, and hardware cost you have. Divide the total by your expected billable hours. This is your baseline. Never go below this number, even for small projects.

faq.question: Should I post my prices on my website?
faq.answer: Most professionals avoid public price lists because every project has different usage requirements. Instead, provide a starting price to filter out clients who do not have the budget for your work.

faq.question: How do I handle clients who push back on my rates?
faq.answer: Explain the value of the usage rights you are granting. If they still refuse, you are likely working with a client that is not a good fit for your business goals.

costs.title: Loss of billable hours
costs.text: Every hour spent arguing about price is an hour you are not creating value.

costs.title: Burnout
costs.text: Underpricing forces you to take on too many projects, leading to exhaustion.

causes.title: Hourly billing trap
causes.text: Charging for time rather than the commercial value of the license.

causes.title: Fear of rejection
causes.text: Using low prices as a shield to prevent potential clients from saying no.

fixes.title: Adopt value-based licensing
fixes.text: Price based on how the client will use your work, not how long it took.

fixes.title: Audit your business
fixes.text: Review your income and expenses to find your true break-even point.
